mainTopic: Foods that may be used for an עירוב: arugula seeds, כשות and חזיז and their ברכות, unripe dates and קור (heart of palm), and the measures for several vegetable foods.
overview: This amud finishes an explanation from the previous amud: the herbs fit for an עירוב are the garden kind. It then explains that arugula seeds count as food because earlier generations ground them as a spice for roast meat. A story follows: a schoolchild tells רבי זירא that כשות gets בורא פרי האדמה and חזיז gets שהכל. The גמרא rules like the child, because ripeness decides the ברכה, and even כשות really feeds from the ground. Next the גמרא challenges רב's ruling that unripe dates (כפניות) cannot be used for an עירוב, using a ברייתא that treats them as food. The final answer is that unripe dates count as food for טומאה only because cooking can sweeten them, a principle of רבי יוחנן about bitter almonds, while an עירוב needs food that is ready to eat. The גמרא then explains how רבי יהודה differs from the תנא קמא about קור (heart of palm): the difference is its ברכה, and the halacha follows שמואל that it is שהכל. Finally, the גמרא gives the measures for כשות, חזיז, the green קליא plant, and fresh beans. It ends with a challenge to raw beets, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The herbs meant are the garden variety
steps.stepSummary: The tail of an earlier explanation: the herbs listed as valid for an עירוב are the cultivated garden kind.
steps.simpleTranslation: …with regard to the garden variety.
steps.whatsHappening: This one word finishes a sentence from the previous section. It tells us the herbs mentioned there are the garden-grown kind.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The earlier discussion needed to know which version of the herbs counts as food. The answer is the cultivated kind, which people actually eat. Wild versions are not normally eaten, so they would not count as food for an עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: Food set aside to establish a shared שבת boundary or domain

steps.confusionAlert: This amud starts in the middle of a sentence. The question being answered appeared on the previous amud, so don't look for it here.

phrases.english: [He was speaking] about the garden variety.
phrases.notes: This finishes the earlier answer: he meant herbs people grow in gardens, which are normal food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a clarification begun on the previous amud.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The herbs referred to are the garden-grown kind.

steps.title: What are arugula seeds good for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how זרע גרגיר can count as food, since people normally eat only the leaves.
steps.simpleTranslation: Arugula seed: what is it fit for?
steps.whatsHappening: The list of foods included arugula seeds, so the גמרא asks what anyone would use them for. This sets up רבי יוחנן's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something can only be used for an עירוב if it is considered food. People usually eat arugula leaves, not seeds. So the גמרא wants to know why the seeds were counted as food at all.

phrases.english: Arugula seed.
What is it fit for?
phrases.notes: A genuine question about how it is used, not an attack.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Picks up an item from the list of foods and asks how it qualifies.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What practical food use arugula seeds have.

steps.title: Arugula seeds were used like pepper
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that earlier generations ground the seeds as a dip for roast meat in place of pepper.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: Because the earlier generations, who had no pepper, would grind it and dip roast meat in it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers the question. The seeds were used as a spice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since people once ground these seeds and ate them as a condiment, they have a recognized food use. That is enough to count them as food, even though it is not their main use.
steps.whatToRemember: Even an unusual but real food use, like a spice, makes an item count as food.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁכֵּן רִאשׁוֹנִים שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לָהֶן פִּלְפְּלִין,
phrases.english: Because the earlier generations, who did not have pepper,
would grind it
and dip roasted meat in it.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Directly answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The seeds were ground into a spice for roast meat, so they count as food.

steps.title: רבי זירא rests at the study hall door
steps.stepSummary: When רבי זירא was worn out from learning, he sat at the entrance of רב יהודה בר אמי's study hall so he could stand for passing חכמים and earn reward.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי זירא was exhausted from his learning, he would go and sit at the entrance of רב יהודה בר אמי. He said: When the חכמים go out and come in, I will stand up before them and receive reward for them.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story about רבי זירא. This step sets the scene for the conversation that follows.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Too tired to learn, רבי זירא still found a way to do a מצוה while resting: honoring תלמידי חכמים by standing up for them. This placement at the door is why he meets the child in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: I will stand up before them

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that standing up for תלמידי חכמים is a מצוה that earns reward.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי זֵירָא כִּי הֲוָה חֲלִישׁ מִגִּרְסֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira, when he was exhausted from his studies,
would go and sit
at the entrance of Rav Yehuda bar Ami.
He said: When the Sages go out and come in,
I will stand up before them
and receive reward through them.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי זֵירָא כִּי הֲוָה חֲלִישׁ מִגִּרְסֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new story. It is connected to the list of עירוב foods because it leads to the ברכה on כשות and חזיז, two items from רב's list (quoted again in Step 28).
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Standing up before תלמידי חכמים is a rewarded מצוה, and רבי זירא used his rest time for it.

steps.title: רבי זירא asks the child what he learned
steps.stepSummary: A schoolchild leaves the study hall, and רבי זירא asks what his teacher taught him.
steps.simpleTranslation: A schoolchild came out. He said to him: What did your teacher teach you?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא asks a passing child what he learned that day. This sets up the child's report in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since he was too tired to learn on his own, רבי זירא picks up some תורה by asking the child. The question itself is simple. The content comes in the child's answer.

keyTerms.meaning: A schoolchild (a child from the house of study)

phrases.english: A schoolchild came out.
He said to him: What did your teacher teach you?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the story from the doorway.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the child had learned from his teacher.

steps.title: The child reports the blessings for dodder and green grain
steps.stepSummary: The child says that כשות gets בורא פרי האדמה and חזיז gets שהכל נהיה בדברו.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: For כשות, 'Who creates the fruit of the ground'; for חזיז, 'By Whose word all things came to be.'
steps.whatsHappening: The child answers by reporting a halacha about ברכות. It gives the blessing for two plants.
steps.deeperAnalysis: כשות is dodder, a parasitic plant that wraps around other plants. חזיז is grain that is still green, cut before it ripens. The teacher gave the 'ground' blessing to כשות and the general שהכל to חזיז.

keyTerms.meaning: Dodder, a parasitic vine that grows on other plants
Blessing for produce of the ground
General blessing, used for foods that do not qualify as proper produce. Some of these foods do grow from the ground.

phrases.english: He said to him: Dodder, 'Who creates the fruit of the ground';
green grain, 'By Whose word all things came to be.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבי זירא's question.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: כשות gets בורא פרי האדמה, and חזיז gets שהכל.

steps.title: רבי זירא argues the blessings should be reversed
steps.stepSummary: רבי זירא objects that the opposite makes more sense. Green grain grows from the ground, while dodder draws its nourishment from the air.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: On the contrary, the reverse is more reasonable. This one grows from the ground, and that one grows from the air.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי זירא challenges what the child learned. He argues each blessing should follow where the plant gets its nourishment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His logic is that a plant feeding from the earth deserves the 'ground' blessing. A plant that hangs on other plants and feeds from the air does not. By that measure, חזיז should get האדמה and כשות should get שהכל, the reverse of what the child said.

keyTerms.meaning: It grows (draws nourishment) from the ground

steps.confusionAlert: The first הַאי ('this one') is the חזיז (green grain), which grows from the ground. The second הַאי is the כשות (dodder), which feeds from the air. The two pronouns go in reverse order from the child's list. This story continues next.

phrases.english: He said to him: On the contrary,
the reverse is more reasonable:
this one (green grain) grows from the ground,
and that one (dodder) grows from the air.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling the child reported.
steps.kashyaTarget: The assignment of בורא פרי האדמה to כשות and שהכל to חזיז.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A blessing should match the source of nourishment. חזיז feeds from the earth and כשות from the air, so the blessings should be reversed.

steps.title: The halacha follows the schoolchild
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rules like the schoolchild. The deciding factor is whether the produce is fully ripened, not where it gets its food.
steps.simpleTranslation: The halacha follows the child from the study hall. Why? This one (כשות) is fully ripened produce, and that one (חזיז) is not fully ripened produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא decides the halacha like the schoolchild and gives the reason.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא thought the ברכה depends on what the plant grows from. The גמרא says the real test is ripeness. כשות is a finished product, so it gets בורא פרי האדמה. חזיז is grain picked before it is ripe, so it only gets שהכל נהיה בדברו.

keyTerms.meaning: a schoolchild of the study hall

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two words. In this סוגיא, כשות (dodder) is the one that is 'fully ripened' and gets האדמה. חזיז (green grain) is the unripe one and gets שהכל.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical rule: the ברכה of בורא פרי האדמה needs produce that is fully developed.

phrases.english: And the halacha is like the child of the study hall.
What is the reason?
This one (dodder) is fully ripened produce,
and that one (green grain) is not fully ripened produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Settles the dispute between the child's teaching and רבי זירא's objection, in the child's favor.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: כשות gets בורא פרי האדמה because it is fully ripened. חזיז gets שהכל because it is not.

steps.title: Dodder also draws nourishment from the ground
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects רבי זירא's claim that כשות grows from the air. It shows that כשות dies when its host shrub is cut.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what you said, 'this one grows from the ground and that one grows from the air' — that is not so. Dodder also grows from the ground. We see that when we cut down the thorn bush, the dodder dies.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now answers רבי זירא's objection head-on and shows that his starting fact is wrong.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי זירא argued that כשות cannot get האדמה because it feeds from the air. The גמרא points out that כשות hangs on a thorn bush and dies when the bush is cut. That means it really feeds from the ground through the bush, just indirectly. So his objection falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: a thorn bush (the host plant of the dodder)

steps.whatToRemember: The child's ruling stands. Ripeness decides the ברכה, and even כשות really draws its food from the ground.

phrases.english: And what you said:
'This one grows from the ground,'
'and that one grows from the air' —
that is not so.
Dodder also grows from the ground,
for we see
that when we cut down the thorn bush,
the dodder dies.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes defending the ruling by knocking out the factual basis of רבי זירא's objection.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: רבי זירא's claim that כשות draws its nourishment from the air.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The factual assumption is wrong. כשות dies when its host bush is cut, so it really feeds from the ground.

steps.title: Challenge: a ברייתא treats unripe dates as food
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions רב's ruling that one may not make an עירוב with כפניות. It quotes a ברייתא that says they can be bought with מעשר שני money and can become טמא as food.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can one really not make an עירוב with unripe dates? But a ברייתא teaches: heart of palm may be bought with מעשר money, but it does not become impure with food impurity. And unripe dates may be bought with מעשר money, and they do become impure with food impurity.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves on to the next part of רב's statement, that one may not make an עירוב with unripe dates, and challenges it with a ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב must be made with food. The ברייתא says כפניות can be bought with מעשר שני money, which may only buy food, and that they can receive טומאת אוכלין, which only applies to real food. So כפניות are real food, and one should be able to make an עירוב with them.

keyTerms.meaning: heart of palm (the soft, edible core of a palm tree)
מעשר שני money, which may only be spent on food
the impurity that applies to foods

phrases.english: And with unripe dates one may not make an eruv?
But it was taught in a baraita:
Heart of palm may be bought with tithe money,
but it does not become impure with food impurity.
And unripe dates may be bought with tithe money,
and they do become impure with food impurity.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic: the next part of רב's list of foods usable for an עירוב.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב's ruling that one may not make an עירוב with כפניות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא treats כפניות as full food for מעשר שני and for טומאת אוכלין, so they should also count as food for an עירוב.

steps.title: רבי יהודה also treats unripe dates as fruit
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues with רבי יהודה. He treats קור as wood, except for מעשר money, and treats כפניות as fruit in every way except that they are exempt from tithes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: Heart of palm is like wood in all its laws, except that it may be bought with מעשר money. And unripe dates are like fruit in all their laws, except that they are exempt from tithes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes quoting the ברייתא. רבי יהודה's view makes the challenge against רב even stronger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה disagrees with the first opinion about קור, but he also calls כפניות fruit 'in all their laws.' Their only exception is the exemption from מעשר, because they are not yet ripe. So both opinions in the ברייתא treat כפניות as real food, which seems to go against רב.

keyTerms.meaning: like wood in all its laws

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: קוֹר הֲרֵי הוּא כְּעֵץ לְכׇל דְּבָרָיו —
phrases.english: Heart of palm is like wood in all its laws,
except that it may be bought with tithe money;

phrases.aramaic: וְכַפְנִיּוֹת הֲרֵי הֵן כִּפְרִי לְכׇל דִּבְרֵיהֶם —
phrases.english: and unripe dates are like fruit in all their laws,
except that they are exempt from tithes.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and adds a second opinion that also supports the challenge.
steps.raayaObject: The claim that כפניות count as real food and should be usable for an עירוב.
steps.raayaSupportSource: רבי יהודה in the ברייתא, who calls כפניות fruit in all their laws.

steps.title: The ברייתא refers to dates that never ripen
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about dates from palms that never ripen. רב was talking about dates that will ripen later.
steps.simpleTranslation: There, the ברייתא is talking about dates that never ripen.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by limiting the ברייתא to a special kind of date.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Some palms never produce ripe dates, so their unripe dates are already the final product and count as full food. רב's ruling is about ordinary dates that are still on the way to ripening, which are not yet considered food. So the ברייתא and רב do not contradict each other.

keyTerms.meaning: dates of palms that never fully ripen

steps.whatToRemember: This answer does not last. Step 13 refutes it, and Step 14 replaces it with a different answer.
steps.confusionAlert: The גמרא is not saying that unripe dates of normal palms are a different kind of food. It is saying that the ברייתא is speaking about a different case, dates that never ripen.

phrases.english: There, it refers to dates that never ripen.
phrases.notes: These palms never produce ripe fruit, so their unripe dates are the final product.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the challenge from the ברייתא by narrowing its case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the case (אוקימתא): the ברייתא is about a specific type of date.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to say that all unripe dates are full food, which would contradict רב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is about dates that never ripen and so are already final fruit. רב is about ordinary dates still in a transitional stage, which cannot be used for an עירוב.

steps.title: רבי יהודה obligates never-ripening fruit in tithes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא attacks the previous answer. If the ברייתא is about dates that never ripen, רבי יהודה could not call them exempt from מעשר, because another ברייתא shows he obligates such fruit in מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, would רבי יהודה say about these that they are exempt from מעשר? But it was taught that רבי יהודה said: the unripe figs of Beityoni were only mentioned for מעשר. The unripe figs of Beityoni and the unripe dates of Tuvina must be tithed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the answer from Step 12. It says that answer cannot work with what we know about רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 12 the גמרא said the ברייתא was about dates from palms that never ripen. But in that ברייתא, רבי יהודה says כפניות are exempt from מעשר. Another ברייתא shows that רבי יהודה obligates never-ripening fruit, like the figs of Beityoni and the dates of Tuvina, in מעשר. So the ברייתא cannot be talking about never-ripening dates.

keyTerms.meaning: If so: introduces a problem that follows from the last answer
Unripe figs from the place called Beityoni, which never fully ripen
Unripe dates from the place called Tuvina, which never fully ripen

steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two ברייתות. The first one (Step 11) has רבי יהודה exempting כפניות from מעשר. The second one, quoted here, has רבי יהודה obligating never-ripening fruit in מעשר. The clash between them is what makes the קשיא.

phrases.english: If so,
phrases.notes: If the ברייתא is about never-ripening dates, as Step 12 said.

phrases.english: in this case, would Rabbi Yehuda say
that they are exempt from tithes?
phrases.notes: A rhetorical question. Surely he would not say this.

phrases.english: But was it not taught: Rabbi Yehuda said:
The unripe figs of Beityoni were not mentioned
except regarding tithes alone.
The unripe figs of Beityoni and the unripe dates of Tuvina
are obligated in tithes.
phrases.notes: Even though they never ripen, they count as full fruit.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, בְּהָא לֵימָא רַבִּי יְהוּדָה פְּטוּרוֹת מִן הַמַּעֲשֵׂר? וְהָתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the תירוץ of Step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that the ברייתא is about dates from palms that never ripen.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רבי יהודה obligates never-ripening fruit in מעשר. So if the ברייתא were about never-ripening dates, he could not call them exempt.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about later-ripening dates, and food impurity is different
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to saying the ברייתא is about dates that will ripen later. They can become טמא as food only because they can be sweetened by cooking, based on רבי יוחנן's principle. That is not enough for an עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the ברייתא is really not about never-ripening dates. The law of food impurity is different, as רבי יוחנן said: since it is fit to be sweetened by fire. Here too: since it can be sweetened by fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא drops its last answer and gives a new one. The dates in the ברייתא are the kind that will ripen, and טומאת אוכלין follows its own rule.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These dates are not edible now, so רב is right that they cannot be used for an עירוב, which needs food that is ready to eat. They can still become טמא as food because cooking can make them edible. Being 'fixable into food' is enough for טומאה, but not for an עירוב.

keyTerms.meaning: Actually / really: returns to an earlier understanding
Fruit of palms that never fully ripen
The ritual impurity that applies to foods
To sweeten them through fire (by cooking)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a key distinction. Something that can become food counts as food for טומאה, but an עירוב needs food that is ready to eat right now.

phrases.english: Rather, actually it is not about never-ripening dates,
phrases.notes: It is about dates that will ripen later, the same kind רב was discussing.

phrases.english: and regarding the impurity of foods, it is different,
as Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וְרָאוּי לְמַתְּקָן עַל יְדֵי הָאוּר,
phrases.english: since it is fit to be sweetened through fire,
phrases.notes: Said originally about מעשר (see Step 15 onward).

phrases.aramaic: הָכָא נָמֵי: הוֹאִיל וְיָכוֹל לְמַתְּקָן עַל יְדֵי הָאוּר.
phrases.english: here too: since it can be sweetened through fire.
phrases.notes: So the dates can become טמא as food.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 13 with a new approach.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing between areas of law (טומאת אוכלין versus עירוב)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Being טמא as food would prove the dates count as food for an עירוב.
steps.terutzMaskana: Food that can be fixed by cooking counts for טומאה, but an עירוב needs food that is ready to eat.

steps.title: Where was רבי יוחנן's statement originally said?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the original setting of רבי יוחנן's 'sweetened by fire' principle.
steps.simpleTranslation: And where was רבי יוחנן's statement said?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a background question: where did רבי יוחנן first say this rule? This sets up the next step, which will quote the source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 borrowed רבי יוחנן's principle. Now the גמרא wants to see its original context to understand it properly.

phrases.english: And where was the statement of Rabbi Yochanan said?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of the principle used in Step 14.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The original context of רבי יוחנן's 'sweetened by fire' principle.

steps.title: The ברייתא about bitter and sweet almonds
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן's statement was said about a ברייתא on tithing almonds. Small bitter almonds and large sweet almonds must be tithed, and the reverse are exempt. רבי שמעון ברבי יוסי reports his father's view in two versions: both kinds of bitter almonds are exempt, or both are obligated.
steps.simpleTranslation: On this, which was taught: bitter almonds: small ones are obligated, large ones are exempt. Sweet ones: large ones are obligated, small ones are exempt. רבי שמעון ברבי יוסי says in his father's name: both are exempt. And some say: both are obligated.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting the ברייתא where רבי יוחנן's rule was first said. The ברייתא is about which almonds need מעשר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Bitter almonds are edible when small and become inedible when large. Sweet almonds are edible only once large. The general rule is that what is edible now must be tithed. רבי יוסי's opinion appears in two versions: both sizes of bitter almonds exempt, or both obligated.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this and that (small and large)

steps.confusionAlert: 'Both this and that' refers to the small and large bitter almonds. It does not mean bitter versus sweet.

phrases.english: On this, which was taught: Bitter almonds —
small ones are obligated, large ones are exempt.
phrases.notes: Small bitter almonds are edible. Large ones are too bitter to eat.

phrases.english: Sweet ones — large ones are obligated, small ones are exempt.
phrases.notes: Small sweet almonds are not yet ripe.

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אוֹמֵר מִשּׁוּם אָבִיו:
phrases.english: Rabbi Shimon son of Rabbi Yosei says in the name of his father:
Both this and that are exempt.
phrases.notes: Both small and large bitter almonds.

phrases.english: And some say: both this and that are obligated.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The ברייתא about tithing bitter and sweet almonds, including the opinion that both sizes of bitter almonds are obligated.

steps.title: רבי חנינא ruled that both are exempt
steps.stepSummary: רבי אילעא reports that רבי חנינא ruled in ציפורי like the version that both sizes of bitter almonds are exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אילעא said: רבי חנינא ruled in ציפורי like the one who says both are exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A practical ruling is added. In real life, רבי חנינא followed the version that exempts both sizes of bitter almonds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This tells us how the matter was decided in practice. The גמרא still goes on to explain the other version, because that is where רבי יוחנן's principle comes from.

keyTerms.meaning: Tzippori, a city in the Galil

phrases.english: Rabbi Ila said:
Rabbi Chanina ruled in Tzippori
according to the words of the one who says both this and that are exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אִילְעָא: הוֹרָה רַבִּי חֲנִינָא בְּצִיפּוֹרִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the practical ruling on the dispute in Step 16.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, both small and large bitter almonds are exempt from מעשר.

steps.title: What are large bitter almonds good for?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks: according to the view that both are obligated, why must large bitter almonds be tithed, if they cannot be eaten?
steps.simpleTranslation: And according to the one who says both are obligated, what are they fit for?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how the 'both obligated' view makes sense. Large bitter almonds seem inedible, and only food needs מעשר. This sets up רבי יוחנן's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מעשר applies only to food. If large bitter almonds cannot be eaten, the גמרא wants to know why that view obligates them.

phrases.english: And according to the one who says both this and that are obligated,
what are they fit for?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר זֶה וָזֶה לְחִיּוּב, לְמַאי חֲזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Questions the reasoning behind the 'both obligated' version in Step 16.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why inedible large bitter almonds would require מעשר.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן: they can be sweetened by fire
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that large bitter almonds count as food for מעשר because cooking can sweeten them. This is the original source of the principle used in Step 14.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said: since they are fit to be sweetened through fire.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוחנן answers that large bitter almonds can be made edible by cooking, so they count as food. This is the source the גמרא was looking for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Something that can be turned into food by cooking already has the status of food for מעשר. The גמרא borrowed this same idea in Step 14 to explain why unripe dates can become טמא as food.
steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן's rule: food that can be made edible by cooking counts as food for מעשר and for טומאת אוכלין. An עירוב is different, because it needs food that is ready to eat now. That is why רב forbids an עירוב with כפניות.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:

phrases.aramaic: הוֹאִיל וְרָאוּי לְמַתְּקָן עַל יְדֵי הָאוּר.
phrases.english: Since they are fit to be sweetened through fire.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן: הוֹאִיל וְרָאוּי לְמַתְּקָן עַל יְדֵי הָאוּר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 18 and completes the source search begun in Step 15.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Large bitter almonds can be sweetened by cooking, so they count as food for מעשר.

steps.title: רבי יהודה's view sounds the same as the first opinion
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes רבי יהודה's statement about קור and points out that it seems identical to the תנא קמא.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: רבי יהודה says, heart of palm is like wood in every way, except that it may be bought with מעשר money. But that is exactly what the first תנא said!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the ברייתא quoted earlier and challenges it. רבי יהודה seems to be saying the same thing as the תנא קמא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא said קור may be bought with כסף מעשר but does not get טומאת אוכלין. רבי יהודה says it is 'like wood' (so it does not get food impurity) but may be bought with כסף מעשר. These look like the same two rules, so why is it presented as a disagreement?

keyTerms.meaning: The soft, edible heart of the palm tree
Second-tithe money, which may only be spent on food
'That is the same as the first opinion' — a challenge that two views seem identical

steps.confusionAlert: Being 'like wood' does not mean you cannot eat it at all. Even רבי יהודה lets you buy it with כסף מעשר, which is only for food. The question is what practical difference he has with the תנא קמא. Steps 21 and 23 answer this.

phrases.english: The Master said:
Rabbi Yehuda says:

phrases.aramaic: קוֹר הֲרֵי הוּא כְּעֵץ לְכׇל דְּבָרָיו,
phrases.english: Heart of palm is like wood in all its aspects,
except that it may be bought with tithe money.
phrases.notes: Second-tithe money may only be used for food, so this treats קור as food in this one respect.

phrases.english: That is the same as the first tanna!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the earlier ברייתא about קור, after the side discussion about almonds and 'sweetened by fire' in Steps 15-19.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ברייתא that presents רבי יהודה as disagreeing with the תנא קמא about קור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Both opinions seem to give the same two rules: no food impurity, but it may be bought with כסף מעשר. So there seems to be no real disagreement.

steps.title: אביי: they disagree about heart of palm that was boiled or fried
steps.stepSummary: אביי answers that the difference is a case where the קור was boiled or fried.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: the difference between them is when someone boiled it or fried it.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers the challenge by finding a case where the two opinions give different results: קור that was cooked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: According to the תנא קמא, once קור is boiled or fried it becomes food and can get טומאת אוכלין. According to רבי יהודה, it is 'like wood in every way,' so even cooking does not make it get food impurity.

keyTerms.meaning: 'There is a difference between them' — the practical case where two views give different results

phrases.english: Abaye said:
If one boiled it or fried it —
there is a difference between them.
phrases.notes: For the תנא קמא, cooked קור gets food impurity. For רבי יהודה, it still does not.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 20's challenge by naming a practical difference between the two opinions.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Finding a practical difference (נפקא מינה) in a specific case
steps.terutzMaskana: They disagree about whether cooked קור gets טומאת אוכלין.

steps.title: רבא: everyone agrees that cooking turns hide into food
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges אביי from a ברייתא that says boiled hide and placenta get food impurity. So no one would say cooked קור stays non-food.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא objected: Is there anyone who says that if one boiled or fried it, it does not get food impurity? But a ברייתא taught: hide and placenta do not get food impurity. But hide that was boiled, and placenta that someone decided to eat, do get food impurity!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks אביי's answer. He brings a ברייתא showing that cooking turns even a non-food item into food for טומאת אוכלין.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Animal hide is normally not eaten, yet once it is boiled it gets food impurity. If something as inedible as hide becomes food through cooking, then cooked קור should become food according to everyone. So אביי's suggested disagreement cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Strongly objected to it' — introduces a forceful challenge to the previous answer
The impurity that applies only to foods
He intended or decided (to eat it), which can give an item the status of food

phrases.english: Rava strongly objected to this:
Is there anyone who says
that if one boiled or fried it, it does not (get food impurity)?
But wasn't it taught in a baraita:
The hide and the placenta
do not contract the impurity of foods.
A hide that one boiled,
and a placenta that one intended to eat —
do contract the impurity of foods!
phrases.notes: So cooking makes even a normally inedible thing count as food.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְקֵיף לַהּ רָבָא: מִי אִיכָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר שְׁלָקוֹ וְטִגְּנוֹ לָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks אביי's answer in Step 21.
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's claim that רבי יהודה holds cooked קור still does not get food impurity
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If boiled hide counts as food for טומאה, then cooked קור must count as food according to everyone. So there is no room for a disagreement about cooked קור.

steps.title: רבא: they disagree about which blessing to make
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives his own answer: the two opinions differ on the ברכה for קור, matching the dispute between רב יהודה and שמואל.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: the difference between them is the ברכה. As it was stated: on heart of palm, רב יהודה says the ברכה is 'בורא פרי האדמה,' and שמואל says it is 'שהכל נהיה בדברו.'
steps.whatsHappening: After rejecting אביי's answer, רבא offers a new practical difference: which ברכה is said before eating קור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא treats קור as a real produce of the ground, so its ברכה is בורא פרי האדמה, like רב יהודה. רבי יהודה says it is 'like wood,' so it is not a normal fruit or vegetable, and its ברכה is only שהכל, like שמואל. This gives a real difference between the two views without contradicting the hide ברייתא.

keyTerms.meaning: 'Who creates the fruit of the ground' — the ברכה on vegetables and produce of the ground
'By Whose word all things came to be' — the general ברכה for foods that are not standard produce

steps.whatToRemember: The two views on קור do not differ about cooking, since cooking makes anything food. They differ about the ברכה: produce of the ground (בורא פרי האדמה) or a general food (שהכל).
steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up רב יהודה the אמורא (who says בורא פרי האדמה) with רבי יהודה the תנא in the ברייתא. רבי יהודה the תנא, who says קור is 'like wood,' actually matches שמואל's שהכל.
steps.whyThisMatters: This connects a טומאה-and-מעשר ברייתא to a practical question of ברכות. It shows how the status of קור as 'wood' or 'produce' affects everyday halacha.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
The difference between them is the blessing.
As it was stated: regarding heart of palm —
Rav Yehuda said: 'Who creates the fruit of the ground,'
phrases.notes: This matches the תנא קמא, who treats קור as produce.

phrases.english: and Shmuel said: 'By Whose word all things came to be.'
phrases.notes: This matches רבי יהודה, who says קור is like wood.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: אִיכָּא בֵּינַיְיהוּ בְּרָכָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces אביי's rejected answer with a new practical difference that answers Step 20's challenge.
steps.terutzResolutionType: New practical difference (נפקא מינה), tied to an existing dispute between אמוראים
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The difference is about cooked קור and טומאת אוכלין (אביי).
steps.terutzMaskana: The difference is the ברכה: the תנא קמא matches רב יהודה (בורא פרי האדמה), and רבי יהודה matches שמואל (שהכל).

steps.title: רב יהודה and שמואל disagree about the blessing on heart of palm
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה says the ברכה on קור is בורא פרי האדמה because it is food. שמואל says it is שהכל because it will eventually harden into wood.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יהודה said: the ברכה is 'Who creates the fruit of the ground,' because it is food. שמואל said: the ברכה is 'By Whose word all things came to be.' Since it will eventually harden, we do not say 'fruit of the ground' over it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now spells out the ברכה dispute that רבא mentioned in the last step. רב יהודה and שמואל each give their ברכה for קור and the reason for it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יהודה looks at what קור is right now: it is edible, so it gets the ברכה of a food from the ground. שמואל looks at where it is heading: it will turn into hard wood, so it does not deserve the ברכה of a fruit and only gets שהכל. This lines up with רבא's answer, where רבי יהודה and the תנא קמא disagree about whether קור counts as a real food.

keyTerms.meaning: The ברכה for produce that grows from the ground
The general ברכה, used for foods that are not a proper 'fruit'

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
'Who creates the fruit of the ground' — it is food.
And Shmuel said:
'By Whose word all things came to be' —
since it will eventually harden,
we do not recite over it 'Who creates the fruit of the ground.'

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר: בּוֹרֵא פְּרִי הָאֲדָמָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Spells out the dispute that רבא's answer in Step 23 depends on.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב יהודה: בורא פרי האדמה, because קור is food now. שמואל: שהכל, because it will eventually harden.

steps.title: שמואל supports רב יהודה's view from radish
steps.stepSummary: שמואל tells רב יהודה that his view makes sense, because radish also hardens eventually and still gets בורא פרי האדמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said to רב יהודה: 'Sharp one, your view makes sense. A radish also eventually hardens, and yet we say "fruit of the ground" over it.'
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל, surprisingly, offers a proof for the opposing view of רב יהודה. He compares קור to radish.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Radish also becomes hard and woody if it is left in the ground, yet we say בורא פרי האדמה on it. So 'it will eventually harden' should not stop קור from getting בורא פרי האדמה either. This directly attacks the reasoning שמואל gave for his own view.

keyTerms.meaning: Sharp one (a term of affection for a student)

phrases.english: Shmuel said to Rav Yehuda:
Sharp one, your view is reasonable,
since a radish will eventually harden,
and we recite over it 'Who creates the fruit of the ground.'

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְרַב יְהוּדָה: שִׁינָּנָא, כְּווֹתָיךְ מִסְתַּבְּרָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a proof for רב יהודה's side of the dispute stated in Step 24.
steps.raayaObject: רב יהודה's view that קור gets בורא פרי האדמה
steps.raayaSupportSource: Radish hardens eventually and still gets בורא פרי האדמה

steps.title: The radish proof is rejected
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. People plant radish so they can eat it soft, but nobody plants a palm tree in order to eat its heart.
steps.simpleTranslation: But it is not so. People plant radish intending to eat it while it is soft. People do not plant palm trees intending to eat the heart of palm.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on שמואל's radish proof and shows that radish and קור are not alike.
steps.deeperAnalysis: What matters is why the plant is grown. Soft radish is the whole purpose of planting radish, so it is a true 'fruit.' A palm is planted for dates, so its heart is only a side product and does not get the fruit ברכה.

keyTerms.meaning: But it is not so (rejecting what was just said)
People plant with the intention of

phrases.english: But it is not so,
people plant radish intending it to be eaten soft;

phrases.aramaic: דִּיקְלָא — לָא נָטְעִי אִינָשֵׁי אַדַּעְתָּא דְקוֹרָא.
phrases.english: a palm tree — people do not plant it intending to eat heart of palm.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְלָא הִיא, צְנוֹן נָטְעִי אִינָשֵׁי אַדַּעְתָּא דְפוּגְלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the radish proof from Step 25.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the radish comparison. The two cases are different.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof ignores the purpose of planting. Radish is grown to be eaten soft, while a palm is not grown for its heart.

steps.title: The halacha follows שמואל
steps.stepSummary: Even though שמואל praised רב יהודה's view, the halacha follows שמואל: the ברכה on קור is שהכל.
steps.simpleTranslation: And even though שמואל praised רב יהודה, the halacha is like שמואל.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the final ruling on the ברכה dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל's compliment does not change the outcome, because the radish proof behind it was just rejected. So the halacha follows שמואל, and the ברכה on קור is שהכל.
steps.whatToRemember: The ברכה on קור (heart of palm) is שהכל, following שמואל. Radish gets בורא פרי האדמה because people plant it in order to eat it soft.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not be thrown by שמואל saying 'your view makes sense' to רב יהודה. That proof was rejected, so the halacha still follows שמואל's own view.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets the practical halacha that heart of palm gets שהכל. It also teaches that the reason a plant is grown can decide its ברכה.

phrases.aramaic: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּקַלְּסֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְרַב יְהוּדָה,
phrases.english: And even though Shmuel praised Rav Yehuda,
the halakha is in accordance with Shmuel.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּקַלְּסֵיהּ שְׁמוּאֵל לְרַב יְהוּדָה, הִלְכְתָא כְּווֹתֵיהּ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the radish proof is rejected in Step 26, the גמרא rules like שמואל.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The ברכה on קור is שהכל, like שמואל.

steps.title: רב's ruling that dodder and green grain work for an עירוב
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא goes back to a statement of רב, quoted by רב יהודה: you may make an עירוב with כשות and חזיז, and their ברכה is בורא פרי האדמה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Returning to the statement itself: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: one may make an עירוב with dodder and green grain, and the ברכה on them is 'Who creates the fruit of the ground.'
steps.whatsHappening: The word גופא tells us the גמרא is going back to a statement mentioned earlier in the discussion so it can look at it more closely. This step sets up the question that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב treats כשות and חזיז as real food. That is why they can be used for an עירוב and why they get בורא פרי האדמה. Now that the full statement is quoted, the גמרא can ask about its details.

keyTerms.meaning: Dodder (a plant that grows on other plants)
Green grain, young stalks not yet ripe

phrases.english: Returning to the matter itself,
Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
dodder and green grain — one may establish an eiruv with them,
and one recites over them 'Who creates the fruit of the ground.'

steps.triggerLanguage: גּוּפָא, אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the קור discussion and goes back to an earlier statement of רב for a closer look.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You may make an עירוב with כשות and חזיז, and their ברכה is בורא פרי האדמה.

steps.title: How much dodder is needed for an עירוב?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what amount of כשות is needed for an עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: How much dodder is needed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a practical follow-up question about רב's ruling: what is the minimum amount of כשות for an עירוב?
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב needs enough food for two meals. כשות is not a normal meal food, so the usual way of measuring does not obviously apply. The גמרא needs a specific measure for it.

phrases.english: Dodder — how much?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the required amount in רב's ruling from Step 28.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The minimum amount of כשות needed for an עירוב.

steps.title: The measure is a handful, like רב יחיאל said
steps.stepSummary: Following what רב יחיאל said about a similar case, the amount of כשות needed is a handful.
steps.simpleTranslation: As רב יחיאל said, a handful. Here too, a handful.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers by borrowing a measure that רב יחיאל gave in a similar case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יחיאל had already set 'a handful' as the measure in a comparable case. The גמרא applies the same measure here, so a handful of כשות is enough for an עירוב.
steps.whatToRemember: An עירוב can be made with כשות. The amount needed is a handful.

phrases.english: As Rav Yeḥiel said:
a handful —
here too, a handful.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question from Step 29.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A handful of כשות, based on רב יחיאל's measure in a similar case.

steps.title: How much green grain is needed for an עירוב?
steps.stepSummary: After giving the amount for כשות, the גמרא asks the same question about חזיז.
steps.simpleTranslation: How much חזיז is needed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks how much חזיז you need to make an עירוב. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב already said that חזיז can be used for an עירוב (step 28). Just as the גמרא asked about the amount of כשות, it now asks about the amount of חזיז.

keyTerms.meaning: Green grain, cut while still young and soft

phrases.english: Green grain, how much is needed?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same question as step 29, now asked about the second food that רב listed
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The amount of חזיז needed for an עירוב

steps.title: A full farmers' bundle
steps.stepSummary: רבה בר טוביה בר יצחק, quoting רב, says the amount is a full farmers' bundle of חזיז.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבה בר טוביה בר יצחק said in the name of רב: As much as fills a farmers' bundle.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers that you need a bundle of חזיז, the size that farmers usually tie.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For חזיז, רב sets a larger measure than the handful used for כשות: a full bundle of the size farmers normally tie. So the two foods in רב's statement get different measures.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר טוֹבִיָּה בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rabba bar Toviya bar Yitzchak said that Rav said:
As much as fills a farmers' bundle.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבָּה בַּר טוֹבִיָּה בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 31

steps.title: An עירוב may be made with glasswort
steps.stepSummary: רב חלקיה בר טוביה says you may make an עירוב with קליא.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חלקיה בר טוביה said: You may make an עירוב with קליא.
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement adds another food to the list. רב חלקיה בר טוביה says קליא may be used for an עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the list included כשות and חזיז. Now קליא is added. As the next step shows, the plain wording of this statement causes a problem.

keyTerms.meaning: Glasswort ash, the burnt plant used to make soap

phrases.english: Rav Chilkiya bar Toviya said:
One may make an eruv with glasswort.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new food to the list of foods that may be used for an עירוב
steps.mimraCoreRuling: An עירוב may be made with קליא

steps.title: Could anyone really eat glasswort ash?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא is surprised: קליא is ash used for soap, so how can it be used for an עירוב?
steps.simpleTranslation: With קליא? Could you really think so?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב חלקיה's statement. קליא ash is not food at all, so it cannot work as an עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב must be made of real food that people eat. Burnt ash used for washing is not food. Read literally, the statement makes no sense.

keyTerms.meaning: Would it enter your mind? (an expression of surprise)

steps.confusionAlert: Do not read this as a question asking for information. The tone is "That can't be right!" It attacks the literal meaning of the statement.

phrases.english: With glasswort, would it enter your mind?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the literal wording of step 33
steps.kashyaTarget: The statement that an עירוב may be made with קליא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: קליא ash is not human food, and an עירוב must be made of food

steps.title: It means the green plant before it is burned
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that the statement refers to the plant from which קליא is made, while it is still green and edible.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, it means the green plant of the קליא.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא fixes the reading. רב חלקיה meant the fresh plant, which people do eat, and not the ash.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before the plant is burned to make soap ash, it is a green vegetable that people can eat. Reading the word "קליא" as the plant solves the problem.

keyTerms.meaning: The green plant of the glasswort, before burning

phrases.english: Rather, with the green plant of glasswort,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 34 by re-reading the statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: קליא means the burnt ash, which is not food
steps.terutzMaskana: קליא means the green, edible plant before burning

steps.title: How much of the green plant is needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what amount of the green קליא plant is needed for an עירוב.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that the food is clear, the גמרא asks how much is needed. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every food used for an עירוב needs a set amount. The גמרא asks the same question it asked about כשות and חזיז.

phrases.english: And how much?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Follows the corrected reading by asking for the amount
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The amount of green קליא plant needed

steps.title: A handful
steps.stepSummary: רב יחיאל says a handful is enough.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יחיאל said: A handful.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with רב יחיאל's measure: a handful of the plant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same measure רב יחיאל gave for the case in step 30. It shows that a handful is the standard amount for these leafy vegetable foods.

keyTerms.meaning: A handful, as much as a hand holds

phrases.english: Rav Yechiel said:
A handful.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 36

steps.title: Villagers ask רבי ירמיה about fresh beans
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה visited some villages. The people asked him whether fresh beans may be used for an עירוב, and he did not know.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה went out to the villages. They asked him: May one make an עירוב with fresh beans? He did not have an answer.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that raises a new question: are fresh, moist beans good for an עירוב? The answer comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Fresh beans are not fully ripe, so one might think they do not count as proper food. Even the great רבי ירמיה did not have a tradition about this.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not have it in hand, he did not know the answer

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya went out to the villages,
they asked him:
What is the law about making an eruv with fresh beans?
He did not have an answer.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new food question through a story
steps.sheelahInformationSought: May fresh beans be used for an עירוב?

steps.title: In the study hall: fresh beans are allowed
steps.stepSummary: When רבי ירמיה returned to the בית מדרש, they told him that רבי ינאי allowed an עירוב with fresh beans.
steps.simpleTranslation: When he came to the בית מדרש, they told him: This is what רבי ינאי said: You may make an עירוב with fresh beans.
steps.whatsHappening: The question from the villages is answered. רבי ינאי's ruling is that fresh beans may be used.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though they are not dried, fresh beans are eaten as food. So they count for an עירוב.

phrases.english: When he came to the study hall,
they said to him:
This is what Rabbi Yannai said:
One may make an eruv with fresh beans.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא לְבֵי מִדְרְשָׁא אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the villagers' question from step 38
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Fresh beans may be used for an עירוב (רבי ינאי)

steps.title: How many fresh beans are needed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what amount of fresh beans is needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how much?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא again asks for the amount, now for fresh beans. The answer follows next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the same pattern as with the other foods. Once a food is allowed, its amount must be set.

phrases.english: And how much?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the amount of the food allowed in step 39
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The amount of fresh beans needed

steps.title: A handful of fresh beans
steps.stepSummary: רב יחיאל again says a handful.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יחיאל said: A handful.
steps.whatsHappening: The answer is the same as before: a handful of fresh beans.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב יחיאל's measure of a handful is used again. It works as a general amount for these fresh foods.
steps.whatToRemember: For כשות, green קליא plant, and fresh beans, the amount for an עירוב is a handful. חזיז is different: it needs a farmers' bundle.

phrases.english: Rav Yechiel said:
A handful.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 40

steps.title: An עירוב may be made with raw beets
steps.stepSummary: רב המנונא says you may make an עירוב with raw beets.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב המנונא said: You may make an עירוב with raw beets.
steps.whatsHappening: Another food is added to the list. רב המנונא allows raw beets for an עירוב.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Beets are a normal food. רב המנונא's point is that they count even when raw. That point is challenged in the next step.

phrases.english: Rav Hamnuna said:
One may make an eruv with raw beets.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a new food to the list
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Raw beets may be used for an עירוב

steps.title: But raw beets are said to be deadly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רב המנונא from רב חסדא, who said raw beet can kill a healthy man.
steps.simpleTranslation: Is that so? But רב חסדא said: Raw beet kills a healthy man!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רב המנונא's ruling. If raw beets are dangerous, they are not proper food, so how can they be used for an עירוב?
steps.deeperAnalysis: An עירוב must be made of food that people normally and safely eat. רב חסדא's statement suggests raw beets are harmful. If so, they should not count. The answer comes on the next amud.
steps.confusionAlert: There is a wordplay here: חַיָּיא means "raw" when it describes the beet and "living/healthy" when it describes the man. Same word, two meanings.

phrases.english: Is that so?
But didn't Rav Chisda say:
A raw beet kills a healthy man!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב המנונא's ruling in step 42
steps.kashyaTarget: רב המנונא's ruling that raw beets may be used for an עירוב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: רב חסדא says raw beets are deadly, so they are not proper food and should not work for an עירוב
